strengths: The paper proposes a simple and interesting approach: iterative DCT-based low-frequency compression of the KV cache, with no added model parameters or architectural modules.
The motivation is plausible and supported by empirical power-spectrum visualizations across layers and heads, showing increasing low-frequency concentration in KV states.
The method is clearly described at a high level and addresses an important practical problem: extending usable context while bounding KV cache size and attention cost.
Experiments cover both language modeling and long-context understanding, including PG-19, Proof-pile, LongBench, and Needle-in-a-Haystack, and include two model families, LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B.

The efficiency analysis is useful: latency and FLOP measurements suggest that the compression overhead itself is small relative to attention computation, and the iterative cache size cap gives clear asymptotic benefits over full-cache attention.
weaknesses: The main empirical comparison is not fully fair or convincing. FreqKV is fine-tuned to use its compressed cache, while several LongBench baselines are inference-time KV compression methods applied to existing models. Improvements may partly come from LongAlpaca SFT rather than the frequency-domain compression mechanism itself.

Important ablations are missing. The paper compares against Dropping only for Needle-in-a-Haystack, but does not systematically compare DCT compression against simple recency, pooling/downsampling, averaging, learned-free low-pass filters, random projections, or other parameter-free compression schemes across all main tasks.

The LongBench gains are mixed rather than uniformly strong. FreqKV improves several QA tasks but degrades others such as MF-en and TREC for LLaMA-2, and Musique, TREC, TriviaQA, SAMSum, and RB-P for LLaMA-3 relative to the base or PyramidKV. The claim of broad superiority is therefore overstated.

The language-modeling comparisons leave gaps: Full FT and LongLoRA results are incomplete at longer evaluation lengths, LoCoCo is only reproduced for limited settings, and full-cache baselines are not always evaluated under matched training lengths, compute budgets, and inference constraints.

The method’s positional treatment is potentially concerning. Compressing keys before RoPE and then assigning compressed pseudo-tokens positions within the cache is pragmatic, but it changes the semantics of token order and distance; the paper gives only limited analysis of when this approximation fails.

Efficiency claims focus on decoding time and FLOPs but do not report peak memory, prefill throughput, wall-clock training cost, or end-to-end serving metrics under realistic batch sizes, which are central for a KV-cache compression paper.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Training details are summarized, but the paper lacks enough implementation detail for chunking, masking, DCT/IDCT variants, cache updates, and exact evaluation protocols to confidently reproduce the reported numbers.

The novelty is moderate. Applying frequency truncation to KV caches is interesting, but the broader idea of low-frequency compression and sequence redundancy removal is well established; the paper needs stronger evidence that this specific formulation is robust and preferable to simpler compression alternatives.

strengths: The core idea is simple and attractive: compress KV states by retaining low-frequency DCT components, with no extra model parameters or architectural modules.
The paper identifies and visualizes an empirical low-frequency concentration phenomenon in KV states across decoder layers, which is a useful diagnostic observation.
The method is evaluated on multiple settings, including LLaMA-2 and LLaMA-3, perplexity on PG-19/Proof-pile, LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and latency/FLOP measurements.
The paper includes some relevant ablations, including retaining ratio, compression before/after RoPE, and comparison to a recency-dropping variant.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for the strength of the claims. Several comparisons are hard to interpret because FreqKV is fine-tuned while many KV-compression baselines are inference-only or use different backbones/settings; the paper does not provide clean controlled comparisons under matched training, cache size, context length, and compute budgets.

Important baselines for long-context extension and efficient inference are missing or underdeveloped, including stronger RoPE/context-extension methods, sliding-window or streaming baselines after the same fine-tuning, and full-cache fine-tuned models evaluated under the same downstream setup.

The main long-context evidence is weaker than claimed. Perplexity is measured with a sliding window of 256, which limits what it can demonstrate about long-range dependency use, and LongBench results are mixed with no aggregate scores or statistical analysis; several tasks degrade relative to the base model or competing methods.

The technical justification is mostly empirical and somewhat shallow. Low-frequency energy concentration does not by itself establish that high-frequency KV components are unimportant for attention behavior, retrieval, positional reasoning, or rare-token information, and the paper gives little analysis of failure modes.

The treatment of positional information is concerning. Compressed vectors are treated like cache tokens and assigned new in-window RoPE positions, but these vectors are mixtures of many original positions; the implications for order-sensitive tasks are not analyzed rigorously.

Efficiency claims focus on decoding latency/FLOPs but omit key practical quantities such as actual KV memory savings, fine-tuning cost, throughput under realistic batching, prefill latency, and behavior with modern optimized attention/cache kernels.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper gives only high-level training settings, lacks code or detailed implementation specifics, omits dataset sample counts for some experiments, and does not report seeds, variance for accuracy benchmarks, or exact prompting/evaluation protocols.

The novelty is moderate at best. Frequency-domain truncation/downsampling is a familiar compression idea, and the paper does not sufficiently distinguish the contribution from prior frequency-domain sequence compression or learned/heuristic KV compression beyond applying DCT to KV caches.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and appealing method for long-context extension: compressing KV caches via low-frequency DCT components and iteratively recompressing as the sequence grows. The approach is parameter-free at inference time and does not require architectural changes, which makes it practically attractive.

The empirical motivation is plausible: the authors show low-frequency energy concentration in key/value states across decoder layers, including a head-wise appendix, and connect this observation directly to the compression design.

The evaluation covers both language modeling and long-context understanding, using LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B, with comparisons against LongLoRA, LoCoCo, SnapKV, PyramidKV, LM-Infinite, and LongHeads. Results are generally strong, especially on PG-19, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and several LongBench tasks.

The efficiency story is convincing at a high level: the method bounds effective cache size, avoids full-cache quadratic growth, and reports latency/FLOP analyses showing negligible compression overhead relative to decoding.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses, including retaining ratio, RoPE placement, decoding latency, FLOPs, and a dropping baseline that helps isolate the value of frequency-domain compression over simple recency retention.
weaknesses: The main novelty is somewhat incremental: frequency-domain truncation and compressed-context mechanisms are well-established ideas, and the paper’s contribution is primarily an effective adaptation to decoder-only KV caches rather than a fundamentally new modeling principle.

The comparison protocol is not fully satisfying. Several baselines are reported from prior work rather than reproduced under identical training data, tuning budgets, cache sizes, and inference implementations, making some headline comparisons difficult to interpret.

The LongBench results are mixed despite the positive framing. FreqKV improves many tasks but also degrades on several important ones, e.g. TREC and TriviaQA for LLaMA-2 and Musique, TREC, TriviaQA, SAMSum, and RB-P for LLaMA-3. The paper does not provide averages, confidence intervals, or enough analysis of failure modes.

The method requires task-specific or long-context fine-tuning, but the cost and sensitivity of this adaptation are under-analyzed. It is unclear how well FreqKV works zero-shot, with fewer tuning steps, across different data mixtures, or for larger and more modern model families.

The treatment of position information is clever but under-justified. Reassigning compressed cache states to positions within the current cache avoids RoPE extrapolation, but the semantic implications of attending to IDCT-compressed pseudo-tokens are not theoretically characterized and may affect tasks requiring precise token-level localization.

The evaluation would be stronger with actual peak memory measurements, throughput under realistic batch sizes, comparisons to sliding-window/attention-sink variants after the same fine-tuning, and more extensive ablations of sink size, retaining ratio, compression frequency, and DCT versus other transforms.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a top-tier submission: implementation specifics for chunk-wise training/inference, exact data preprocessing, hardware-normalized throughput, and code availability are not clearly established in the manuscript.

strengths: Proposes a simple and appealing KV-cache compression idea: applying DCT along the sequence dimension, retaining low-frequency KV components, and iteratively recompressing older context while preserving sink/recent tokens.

The method is lightweight at inference, architecture-agnostic in principle, and does not introduce additional compressor parameters; the reported compression overhead is small relative to attention compute.

The paper includes a broad empirical study across language modeling, LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and LongGenBench, plus useful ablations on frequency band choice, retaining ratio, sink size, RoPE handling, rescaling, and FLOPs.
The frequency-domain motivation is intuitive and supported by power-spectrum visualizations and ablations showing low-frequency retention is much better than high-frequency retention.
weaknesses: The central context-extension mechanism is not fully justified technically: compressed states are assigned new cache positions rather than original positions, which may substantially distort positional semantics. The paper gives empirical evidence but little analysis of when this approximation is valid or failure modes.

Several headline comparisons are not fully fair or convincing. Many baselines are applied beyond their intended/native positional range and collapse at 16K, while FreqKV is fine-tuned for its compression pattern; stronger adapted long-context baselines and RoPE-scaling methods are missing.

Claims of robust 256K extension rely mainly on PG-19 perplexity with a sliding window, which is a weak test of long-range retrieval and reasoning. There is no 256K retrieval, QA, or generation evaluation, so the strongest extrapolation claim is under-supported.

The method is described as parameter-free, but the main reported performance uses fine-tuning/LoRA adaptation. The distinction between parameter-free inference and training-dependent adaptation should be clearer, and zero-shot performance is not sufficiently characterized.

Results are mixed in places: on LongBench the gains over full cache or strong baselines are often modest, and on Proof-pile FreqKV trails full-cache LongLoRA at longer lengths, suggesting sensitivity to local symbolic information.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript text: the abstract has an unfinished code URL, many comparisons are partly reproduced and partly taken from prior work, and there are no variance estimates, significance tests, or detailed generation/evaluation decoding settings for some benchmarks.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and potentially useful idea: compress KV caches by retaining low-frequency DCT components and iteratively recompressing older context, which is easy to implement and architecture-agnostic in principle.

The manuscript includes several relevant evaluations across language modeling, LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack, LongGenBench, latency, training cost, and ablations on retaining ratio, sink size, high-vs-low frequency retention, and rescaling.
The empirical observation that KV states show low-frequency energy concentration is interesting and gives some motivation for exploring frequency-domain cache compression.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not convincing enough for the strength of the claims. Many long-context understanding comparisons appear unfair because FreqKV receives task-specific adaptation/fine-tuning for context extension, while several KV eviction baselines are largely inference-time methods and are evaluated in regimes where they predictably fail due to out-of-bound RoPE handling. This makes the large gains on RULER and Needle-in-a-Haystack difficult to interpret.

The central claim of robust extension to 256K is supported mainly by perplexity on PG-19 with a sliding window, which is a weak test of long-range information use. There is no convincing downstream evaluation at very long lengths showing retrieval, reasoning, or generation quality beyond 16K.

The paper repeatedly claims that FreqKV preserves information from all tokens, but truncating DCT coefficients and treating reconstructed compressed states as pseudo-tokens is lossy and changes positional/attention semantics. The technical discussion does not adequately analyze what information is lost or when the approximation should be valid.

Novelty is moderate at best. Frequency-domain compression and low-frequency retention are established ideas, and the paper does not provide a deep theoretical or algorithmic advance beyond applying DCT truncation to KV states with iterative recompression.

The strongest LongBench improvements are relatively small in average score, and some categories degrade compared with full cache or strong baselines. The paper’s broad “SOTA” and “consistently outperforms” language overstates mixed results.

The method is described as parameter-free, but the reported main results rely on LoRA/continued training or SFT to adapt the model to the compression pattern. The distinction between parameter-free inference mechanism and training-dependent performance should be made much clearer.

Important baselines are missing or underdeveloped for context extension, such as strong RoPE scaling/interpolation methods combined with efficient attention/cache strategies, recurrent/compressive memory baselines, and trained compression methods under matched training budgets.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone: the abstract says code is available but no URL is provided, and several comparison results are reproduced from official code without enough detail to assess whether prompts, budgets, compression ratios, fine-tuning, and cache sizes are matched.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and appealing idea: compressing KV caches by retaining low-frequency DCT components, with an iterative scheme that naturally gives more fidelity to recent context. The method is parameter-free at inference, architecture-agnostic in principle, and easy to integrate compared with approaches requiring extra compressor modules.

The empirical evaluation is broad and largely convincing. Results cover language modeling, long-context understanding, needle retrieval, RULER, LongBench, and long-generation benchmarks, with comparisons to many recent KV compression baselines.

The paper provides useful analysis supporting the design choices, including power-spectrum observations, high- vs low-frequency ablations, retaining-ratio studies, sink-token ablations, RoPE placement analysis, and compression-overhead measurements.

Efficiency is a clear strength. The method appears to reduce memory and training cost while keeping compression overhead negligible relative to decoding/prefilling costs, and the 256K extrapolation results are promising.
The writing is generally clear, and the algorithmic description is sufficiently detailed to understand the method.
weaknesses: The central claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence. Although the method is described as parameter-free, most strong results rely on fine-tuning/adaptation; the zero-shot or no-training behavior is not sufficiently characterized across the main benchmarks.

Some comparisons may not be fully fair or maximally informative. Several baselines are evaluated in ways that cause RoPE out-of-window collapse, while FreqKV avoids this by compressing pre-RoPE and reallocating positions. It is unclear whether stronger baseline variants with compatible position handling, interpolation, or similar fine-tuning would narrow the gap.

The 256K extrapolation result is compelling but mostly shown via perplexity on PG-19 validation/test-style settings. More retrieval, reasoning, and generation evaluations at ultra-long lengths would be needed to substantiate robust long-context extension rather than stable language-modeling loss.

The method may discard important high-frequency/local details, as acknowledged by weaker Proof-pile results. This limitation could matter for code, math, structured data, exact copying, and tasks requiring token-level fidelity, but the paper does not deeply explore these failure modes.

The conceptual interpretation that low frequencies encode global semantics and high frequencies encode local details is plausible but not fully established. The synonym perturbation experiment is suggestive, but limited and not enough to strongly support the semantic decomposition claim.

Reproducibility would benefit from more implementation detail on chunking, DCT/IDCT numerical choices, cache layout, and exact baseline tuning/evaluation settings, especially since small implementation choices could affect long-context performance.
